evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Multiconfiguration assemblies of Nitinol strands, wires, and steel wire ropes can produce three distinct constitutive behaviors: strong hardening pinched hysteresis, quasi-linear softening, and an intermediate pinched-hardening response depending on boundary constraints and strand stiffness ratios.

The combination of geometric rope stretching, interwire friction, and thermoelastic martensitic phase transformations produces pinching at the origin of force-displacement loops and residual strain upon complete unloading.

An extended Bouc-Wen phenomenological model incorporating a two-parameter bell-shaped pinching function accurately characterizes the origin-pinched hysteretic restoring force across diverse strand assemblies.
The uniaxial tensile hysteretic response of superelastic Nitinol wires and seven-wire strands is accurately identified using the one-dimensional Ivshin-Pence constitutive model.
Seven-wire Nitinol strands exhibit lower axial stress per unit area at equivalent strain than single straight wires because of pitch length extension under tension and interwire frictional sliding.

Differential evolution metaheuristic optimization successfully identifies constitutive parameters for pinched hysteretic systems without needing objective function gradients or initial linearization points.

constitutive_assumptions: Isotropic material behavior for the shape memory alloy (SMA).
Isothermal conditions during superelastic loading and unloading cycles.

Auricchio superelastic constitutive model defining forward and reverse stress-induced phase transformations using four threshold stress values (starting/final forward transformation stresses, starting/final reverse transformation stresses) and maximum residual strain.

Coupled sections in the simplified FE model act like rigid cross-sections where relative translational displacements of nodes within the section are constrained to zero, while nodes outside remain unaffected and uncoupled.
Squeezing effects and contact behavior between adjacent outer wires are omitted in the simplified FE model.
SMA wires remain in the elastic/superelastic regime, mitigating some computational errors introduced by omitting wire-to-wire squeezing.
control_variables: SMA chemical composition: 55.5 wt% Ni, ~44.477 wt% Ti, with trace elements (C 0.011 wt%, Cu 0.003 wt%, Co < 0.003 wt%, Cr < 0.003 wt%, Nb < 0.003 wt%).

SMA material parameters: elastic modulus E = 1.33 × 10^4 MPa, phase transition temperature = -10 °C, tensile strength = 1530 MPa, elongation = 22.18%, transformation stresses (starting forward = 400 MPa, final forward = 600 MPa, starting reverse = 300 MPa, final reverse = 100 MPa), maximum residual strain = 0.22.
Cable construction: 7-wire strand (1 straight core wire and 6 outer helical wires); 7×7 wire rope (7 strands, 49 wires).
Outer strand pitch length Lp2 for the 7×7 wire rope held constant at 80 mm.
Normal stiffness factor of 0.8 for contact elements in the refined FE model.
dependent_variables: Hysteresis loop shape and outer hysteresis loop area (energy dissipation capacity).
Tensile force corresponding to the upper horizontal transformation plateau segment.
Von Mises stress distributions across central and outer wires or strands.
Initial stiffness of the strand or rope.
Ductility of the strand compared to individual wires.
Computational solution time and numerical convergence rate.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A simplified FE modeling method using coupled nodal cross-sections at periodic intervals eliminates contact elements, reducing computational run time from 23 hours to approximately 30 minutes while closely reproducing the hysteretic response of refined contact models.

Varying the pitch length (Lp1) of superelastic SMA strands has negligible influence on the hysteresis loop area (energy dissipation changes remain within 5.8%), whereas increasing pitch length raises the tensile force of the upper horizontal transformation segment.
Superelastic SMA strands achieve greater ductility than single SMA wires because outer helical wires remain elastic while the central core wire transitions into the strain hardening phase.

For the simplified FE modeling approach, numerical accuracy is maintained when the interval between coupled sections (Δl) is less than one-fifth of the pitch length, and a model length of one-eighth the pitch length is sufficient for analysis.

In 7×7 SMA wire ropes under axial tension, individual strand pitch length (Lp1) has negligible effect on the overall hysteresis loops, with the central core strand sustaining 13.3% higher stress than outer strands.
SMA strands and ropes exhibit weak bending stiffness and pseudoelastic energy dissipation, presenting potential utility in flexible damping, isolation, and self-centering applications.

experimental_setup: Uniaxial tensile stress-strain characterization of superelastic NiTi SMA wire (diameter approximately 0.5 mm, provided by Gaohan metal materials Co. Ltd., Guangdong, China) used to calibrate constitutive material parameters for numerical simulations; the paper is predominantly numerical and does not detail a physical experimental test apparatus for multi-wire strands or ropes.
independent_variables: Pitch length of the wire strand (Lp1: 10 mm, 20 mm, 40 mm, and infinity/parallel wires).
Pitch length of wires in 7×7 wire rope (Lp1: 80 mm, 160 mm, 320 mm).
Distance between adjacent coupled sections (Δl: 2 mm, 4 mm, 8 mm).
Finite element model length (l: 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm, 40 mm).
Finite element modeling methodology (simplified coupled-section model vs. refined contact-element model using CONTA174 and TARGE170).
Rope lay configuration (regular lay vs. lang lay).
limitations_inferred: The study relies almost exclusively on numerical finite element models without full-scale experimental cyclic tension testing of multi-wire strands or 7×7 ropes to experimentally validate simulated hysteresis loops.
The analysis is restricted to monotonic and cyclic pure axial tension, omitting bending, torsional, or multi-axial loading states relevant to flexible robotic joints or continuum mechanisms.
Inter-wire friction and relative sliding dissipation are omitted in the simplified coupled-section model.
Thermal effects, strain-rate dependencies, and latent heat generation during cyclic transformation are not evaluated due to the isothermal assumption.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The simplified numerical model neglects the squeezing effect between outer and inner wires, reducing the stress on inner wires and potentially introducing computational error.
Coupling translational degrees of freedom at coupled sections creates localized errors in stress distribution restricted to the coupled sections.
Contact behavior between adjacent outer wires is not considered in the refined FE model.
Setting the distance between adjacent coupled sections (Δl) excessively large prevents effective wire constraint and degrades the initial stiffness of the cable model.
Numerical scale was limited to a 7×7 wire rope (49 wires) due to computational power requirements.
main_results: The simplified FE model matches the hysteresis loop of the refined contact model while lowering computation time from 23 hours to about 30 minutes and preventing numerical non-convergence.
Pitch length (Lp1) has negligible impact on the hysteresis loop area of SMA strands, with total area variation staying within 5.8%.
Tensile force corresponding to the forward transformation upper horizontal segment increases as pitch length Lp1 increases.
SMA strands demonstrate higher ductility than individual SMA wires because the outer helical wires remain elastic when the central wire enters the hardening stage.
In 7×7 SMA wire ropes, pitch length Lp1 has almost no influence on hysteresis behavior or tensile force, and stress in the central strand is 13.3% higher than in outer strands.

Numerical accuracy for the simplified model is preserved if the coupled section interval Δl is less than 0.2 times the pitch length, and an FE model length of one-eighth the pitch length yields satisfactory results.
modeling_methods: Finite element (FE) modeling and numerical analysis in ANSYS.
Refined 3D solid FE model using surface-to-surface contact elements (CONTA174 on central wire surface and TARGE170 on outer wire surfaces).
Simplified FE model using coupled sections that couple translational degrees of freedom of cross-sectional nodes at spacing Δl without contact elements.
Auricchio 3D superelasticity material formulation (accessed via TB, SMA in ANSYS).
performance_metrics: Hysteresis loop area and percentage variation in energy dissipation capacity (within 5.8%).
Computation time (reduction from 23 h to 30 min).
Tensile force at the upper transformation plateau.
Von Mises stress magnitude and stress ratio between core and outer strands (central strand 13.3% higher).
Ductility comparison between strands and individual wires.
Initial stiffness of the strand or rope.
possible_gap_implications: The coupled-section modeling methodology could provide a computationally efficient framework for simulating multi-wire superelastic SMA tendons or cable bundles in soft and continuum robotics without contact non-convergence.

The decoupling of energy dissipation area from pitch length suggests that strand geometry can be tailored for higher ductility or tailored plateau tension in flexible damping mechanisms without sacrificing cyclic energy absorption, though validation under robotic bending conditions is required.
paper.research_objective: To reveal the hysteresis behavior of shape memory alloy (SMA) strands and ropes, investigate the influence of pitch length on their mechanical performance, and develop a simplified finite element model that avoids contact elements to facilitate the numerical analysis of large-scale SMA wire ropes.
paper.research_problem: Numerical modeling of large-scale SMA wire ropes and strands is computationally prohibitive, highly nonlinear, and prone to non-convergence due to the necessity of defining inter-wire contact elements between dozens of adjacent slender helical wires.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A three-dimensional phenomenological constitutive formulation (Souza model) implemented via UMAT in Abaqus captures the mechanical response of single-helix and double-helix SMA wire ropes under both superelasticity and shape memory effect conditions.

Finite element analysis of a 1x37 steel wire rope under axial forces from 10 kN to 35 kN accurately reproduces benchmark numerical elongation results with relative errors below 2%, confirming the validity of the interwire contact and kinematic coupling approach.
Simulations of 7x7 and 1x27 superelastic SMA wire ropes match published experimental normal and shear stress-strain behaviors with average discrepancies of 20% to 25%.

Axial loading of helical SMA cables induces significant internal shear stresses and torsional torques due to strand helicity, with the sign of shear stress directly dictated by the wire lay direction (left-handed versus right-handed lay).

In shape memory effect cables deformed below As, interwire contact and friction lead to residual normal and shear stresses upon unloading, which are subsequently recovered through reverse phase transformation upon heating above Af within a narrow temperature and time range.

Core wires experience the highest normal stress due to their smaller cross-sectional area but withstand the lowest axial force, whereas outer double-helix wires (such as D-type wires in 7x7 cables) bear the largest portion of the total axial load.
Factorial design of experiments and response surface methodology show that maximizing the specific energy of an SME wire rope requires increasing the wire diameter and reducing the helix angle.

experimental_setup: No original physical experiments were conducted in this study; the authors performed finite element simulations using Abaqus/Standard (implicit solver) with a user-defined material subroutine (UMAT).

Validation used published experimental test data from Reedlunn et al., where cable ends were clamped between steel plates using pneumatic clamps, axial displacement was imposed at one end, and temperatures were recorded via thermocouples.
Validation for the contact mechanics modeling used published numerical benchmark results for a 1x37 steel wire rope by Stanova et al.
Optimization employed a 3^2 factorial design of experiment consisting of 32 finite element simulation runs analyzed via Design-Expert software.
independent_variables: Wire rope geometric configuration (single-helix 1x27 vs. double-helix 7x7)
Thermomechanical operating regime (superelastic behavior at T > Af vs. shape memory effect behavior at T < As with subsequent heating above Af)
Radial position / component layer within the strand (core wire A, inner layer B, intermediate layer C, outer layer D)
Wire diameter D (evaluated at 0.10, 0.20, and 0.38 mm during optimization)
Helix angle phi (evaluated at 54.9°, 63.0°, and 72.0° during optimization)
Applied tensile load / axial displacement
limitations_inferred: The investigation is entirely numerical and relies strictly on third-party published data for empirical comparison without primary experimental testing.

Thermomechanical coupling (such as self-heating or latent heat release during rapid phase transformation) is not dynamically resolved, assuming essentially isothermal or prescribed temperature fields.
Cyclic degradation, fatigue life, fretting wear between wires under repeated loading, and functional fatigue of the SMA were not evaluated.

Simulated cable lengths were limited to minimal pitch lengths (4 mm for 1x27 and 10 mm for 7x7) to ensure full strand rotation while managing computational cost, which may not capture full-scale boundary friction effects.
Integration or physical realization of these cables as soft robotic actuators or continuum mechanisms was not demonstrated.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The implicit finite element solution method employed is computationally complex and time-consuming compared to explicit solvers.
End clamping and pressing conditions that restrict wire rotation about the longitudinal axis in physical experiments were neglected in the numerical boundary condition setup.
Tension-compression asymmetry of the shape memory alloy material was not incorporated into the constitutive model.
Numerical predictions exhibited an average difference of 20% for normal stress and 25% for shear stress compared to experimental data for the 7x7 cable, and up to 25% difference for the 1x27 cable.
To reduce simulation run times in the factorial optimization, identical wire diameters were assumed for core and twisted wires, restricting the number of explored design factors.
main_results: The finite element modeling framework successfully captured multi-wire contact and kinematic behavior, matching 1x37 steel cable benchmark data with under 2% error across tensile loads from 10 to 35 kN.

Superelastic SMA cable models reproduced experimental stress-strain trends with average deviations of 20% to 25%, showing that phase transformation yields substantial normal strains across cable components.

Axial loading induces coupled torsional torques and shear stresses in both 1x27 and 7x7 cables, with shear stress magnitude significantly higher in 1x27 due to its larger helix angle, and shear stress sign directly governed by strand lay direction.

In both SE and SME cables, core wires sustain the highest normal stresses (up to ~330 MPa in 7x7 and ~680 MPa in 1x27 SME cables) because of their low cross-sectional area, but they carry the smallest share of total axial force.

Outer wires with double-helix twisting (D-type wires in 7x7 cables) sustain lower normal and shear stresses but carry the largest portion of total axial force (~260 N) owing to their dominant collective cross-sectional area.

Upon unloading SME wire ropes at temperatures below As, interwire friction and contact generate residual stresses (~100 MPa in the 7x7 core wire), which together with inelastic strains recover rapidly upon heating above Af.

Statistical response surface optimization demonstrated that cable specific energy increases with larger wire diameter and smaller helix angle, identifying an optimal configuration at D = 0.38 mm and phi = 54.9°.

Design of experiments (3^2 factorial design and response surface methodology using Design-Expert software)

Normal stress-strain response (MPa vs. strain)

possible_gap_implications: Because axial tension in helical SMA wire ropes induces significant internal shear stresses and torsional coupling, deploying SMA cables as soft robotic tendons or continuum actuators will require accounting for twisting and transverse contact stresses.

The presence of significant residual stresses and interwire friction during unloading highlights that hysteresis and internal friction must be integrated into control models for SMA cable-driven mechanisms.

Neglecting tension-compression asymmetry and realistic boundary clamping resulted in up to 25% discrepancy with experimental tests, indicating that higher-fidelity constitutive formulations are needed for precision soft robotic applications.
Fretting wear, interwire friction degradation, and cyclic thermomechanical fatigue remain unaddressed, posing an open research question for durable soft robotic actuation.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The restoring force of a NiTiNOL wire rope can be formulated by combining a physical beam constraint model for elastic geometric stiffness and a modified Bouc-Wen model with an exponential function for pinched hysteretic damping.

The generalized equivalent stiffness displays a stiffness-softening-hardening profile, where initial stiffness is primarily governed by the pinching parameter xi, small-displacement softening by Bouc-Wen sum (beta + gamma), and large-displacement hardening by cubic stiffness k3.

The rate-independent generalized equivalent damping ratio varies non-monotonically, first increasing and then decreasing with displacement amplitude due to the combined Bouc-Wen hysteresis and pinching effect.

Compared to an isolator with a steel wire rope, the NiTiNOL wire rope isolator possesses lower initial stiffness and higher equivalent damping, preventing unbounded resonant responses and providing superior broadband vibration isolation.

Both peak displacement transmissibility and resonant frequency vary non-monotonically with excitation amplitude, defining optimal excitation amplitudes for resonance suppression (Ab-pmin) and for low-frequency isolation (Ab-rmin).

Harmonic balance method using alternating frequency/time domain formulation closely matches Runge-Kutta numerical integration for the modified Bouc-Wen model, although third-order truncation excludes superharmonic resonances.

Analytical predictions show general agreement with experimental swept-frequency acceleration response data from a NiTiNOL wire rope damper, though both the analytical model and Runge-Kutta numerical integration fail to reproduce the experimentally observed softening at 7.68 m/s^2.

experimental_setup: No primary experimental apparatus was built or tested by the authors in this study.

For model verification, secondary experimental data from previously published literature (Carboni and Lacarbonara, 2016) was used, involving swept-frequency base acceleration tests (at 6.35 m/s^2 and 7.68 m/s^2) on a damper comprising horizontal symmetric NiTiNOL wire ropes without a vertical spring.

Base excitation frequency wb (dimensionless frequency ratio eta)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A 3D geometrically non-linear finite element model with penalty contact and Coulomb friction was formulated to capture the combined tension, radial pressure, and bending behavior of helically-interwound cores, profile fillers, and sheath layers.

Relative slip between helically wound power cores and the adjacent sheath occurs almost exclusively in the loxodromic (axial) direction due to the small lay-angle, closely matching analytical loxodromic kinematic predictions.

Polymeric profile fillers undergo significant longitudinal shear deformation (up to ~1% shear strain) during cyclic bending, which delays and slows the build-up of friction stresses at low to moderate curvatures.
Internal load-sharing between helically interwound components results in slightly less than one-third of the total inner sheath contact lineload being transmitted to each individual power core.

Analytical models based on loxodromic curves without filler compliance predict a higher axial stress range and faster stress transitions during bending reversals than 3D FE simulations, demonstrating conservatism in analytical stress predictions.

Analytical formulations do not accommodate the longitudinal displacement mismatch and opposite-direction sliding of adjacent helically-interwound cores, which leads to earlier slipping than analytically predicted.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Unbraided single NiTi shape memory alloy wire exhibits a narrow internal friction damping peak near its martensitic transformation temperature (maximum tanδ ~0.13), with storage modulus dropping from ~61 GPa to ~20 GPa and low damping in single-phase martensite (~0.05) or austenite (~0.001).

Braided NiTi microfilament architectures convert the narrow phase transformation damping peak into a broad, temperature-insensitive damping plateau over a temperature window exceeding 145 °C (-70 °C to 75 °C) while significantly lowering storage modulus.

Double-braided 88B microfilaments achieve a high tanδ (0.06 to 0.11) and low storage modulus (~3.6 GPa cooling, ~4.3 GPa heating) over a >145 °C window, with overlapping modulus and tanδ curves at 1 Hz and 5 Hz.

Single-braided 8B microfilaments display a stable tanδ of 0.02 to 0.05 and storage modulus of ~11 to 12 GPa across 145 °C, maintaining nearly identical damping response over 10 cooling-heating cycles.

Individual NiTi wires in the braided architecture follow helical paths forming a micro-spring network that converts structural deformation into localized bending, torsion, and inhomogeneous stresses, inducing sequential localized martensitic transformations alongside inter-wire contact micro-sliding friction dissipation.

Increasing wire count from 4 to 8 and 12 wires at 50 ppi increases inter-wire contact sites and interwoven micro-springs, raising tanδ from 0.008-0.02 (4B) to 0.03-0.06 (12B), with storage modulus remaining between 17 and 22 GPa.

Varying braiding density in 8-wire microfilaments shows that low density (ppi25) retains an intrinsic transformation damping peak (~0.10 near -20 °C) due to weak structural constraints, whereas high density (ppi80) flattens tanδ to 0.02-0.04 because tight geometric constraints restrict axial extension and bending, thereby shortening micro-slip displacement.

At low braiding density (ppi25), structural constraint is relatively weak, retaining intrinsic phase transformation peaks and temperature dependence (Page 4).

At high braiding density (ppi80), tight geometric constraints restrict axial extension and bending, shortening micro-slip displacement and attenuating frictional dissipation and overall damping capacity despite a higher number of contact sites (Page 4).
main_results: Braiding NiTi microfilaments transformed the narrow martensitic transformation internal friction peak into a broad, temperature-insensitive damping plateau over a temperature range exceeding 145 °C (-70 °C to 75 °C).
Double-braided 88B microfilaments achieved a tanδ of ~0.06 to 0.11 and an ultra-low storage modulus of ~3.6 GPa (cooling) to ~4.3 GPa (heating) across the 145 °C window.

Single-braided 8B microfilaments demonstrated stable tanδ (0.02 to 0.05), storage modulus of ~11 to 12 GPa, near-perfect cyclic stability over 10 thermal cycles, and frequency insensitivity between 1 Hz and 5 Hz.

constitutive_assumptions: Linear relationship between forward/reverse phase transformation start stresses and temperature governed by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation (CM and CA coefficients).
Equivalent linear viscoelastic element assumption for evaluating the equivalent viscous damping factor (ξ) from dissipated energy and stored elastic energy.
Nominal engineering stress calculated using the initial undeformed cross-sectional area across progressive individual filament failures.
Uniform axial tension along the 30 mm gauge length between grips.

Ambient room temperature (22 ± 2 °C)
Tensile strain amplitude range (5% peak-to-peak, oscillating between 2.5% and 7.5% strain)
Pre-strain level (5.0% strain)
Pre-cycling conditioning protocol (128 cycles at 0.25 Hz to stabilize superelastic behavior)
Sinusoidal loading waveform
Equivalent nominal cross-sectional area between the 1 × 7 micro cable and the solid reference wire

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Repeated cyclic loading above a critical self-heating frequency causes latent heat accumulation, elevating internal temperature and shifting transformation stresses upward according to the Clausius-Clapeyron law, which stiffens the SMA element during dynamic cycling.

The 1 × 7 NiTi micro cable displays a lower self-heating critical frequency (0.99 Hz) and higher temperature increase (80% increase after 128 cycles at 10 Hz) compared to a solid reference wire (1.76 Hz and 52% increase), attributed to inter-filament friction heat generation.

Multi-filament micro cable geometry achieves higher dissipated energy and damping capacity (15% to 30% higher ED and 20% to 47% higher ξ) than a monolithic wire of equivalent area due to additional friction between twisted filaments.
Dissipated energy per cycle and damping ratio degrade with increasing cycle count and increasing dynamic frequency across both micro cables and solid wires.

The multi-filament micro cable exhibits a shorter fatigue life to first filament failure than a solid wire due to inter-strand fretting friction and manufacturing dimples, but provides progressive redundancy and delayed complete failure through sequential breakage of individual wires.

experimental_setup: 1 × 7 NiTi superelastic micro cable (outer diameter 0.4064 mm, composed of six 0.1354 mm outer wires twisted at a -15° helix angle around a straight core wire; nominal 55 wt.% Ni, EDS measured 53.8 wt.% Ni).
Monolithic superelastic NiTi reference wire (0.35 mm diameter) with equivalent total cross-sectional area.
ElectroPuls E10000 electrical dynamic testing machine (INSTRON) equipped with a 10 kN load cell, operated under strain control.
K-type micro thermocouple (100 µm diameter) affixed with adhesive to the outer surface of the specimen, recorded by an HBM Quantum X data acquisition system at 100 Hz.
TA Instruments Q800 Dynamic Mechanical Analyzer (DMA) for isothermal tensile testing of single core wire (12.6 mm gauge length, 0.5%/min strain rate, 35 °C to 85 °C).
TA Instruments Q20 Differential Scanning Calorimeter (DSC) for transformation temperatures (-60 °C to 100 °C, 10 °C/min rate under nitrogen).
TESCAN VEGA3 Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) with BSE detector and Oxford Instruments X-act Energy Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS).

Number of loading cycles (1 to 128 cycles for thermomechanical evaluation; up to ~6000 cycles for fatigue life)

limitations_inferred: Dynamic mechanical testing was performed exclusively under uniaxial tension, leaving bending, torsional, or multi-axial loading uncharacterized.
Surface thermocouple measurement at a single external location may not accurately capture internal radial temperature gradients inside the twisted multi-filament bundle.
Only a single pre-strain (5%) and strain amplitude (5% peak-to-peak) were evaluated dynamically, without exploring performance under smaller or larger strain amplitudes.
No active robotic system, soft actuator, or continuum manipulator was constructed or tested with the micro cables.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The distance between grips was set equal to the 30 mm gauge length due to sample limitations, differing from the ASTM F2516 standard recommendation of at least 150 mm grip separation for wire diameters ≤ 0.2 mm.
The 128 cycles utilized during frequency sweep testing were insufficient to reach steady-state thermal equilibrium.
The structural fatigue evaluation was preliminary, lacking statistical analysis across multiple samples.
Manufacturing-induced surface defects, such as dimples, were observed on the micro cables, contributing to reduced structural fatigue life.
main_results: The critical self-heating frequency (fc) was determined as 0.99 Hz for the NiTi micro cable and 1.76 Hz for the solid reference wire.

Above fc, accumulation of latent heat and inter-wire friction raised specimen temperature (e.g., reaching 49.25 °C at 10 Hz after 128 cycles for the micro cable, an 80% increase relative to 0.25 Hz), leading to upward shifting of superelastic loops and strain hardening due to the Clausius-Clapeyron relation.
Dissipated energy per cycle (ED) and equivalent damping factor (ξ) decreased with increasing cycling and loading frequency, dropping by up to ~45-50% at 10 Hz compared to 1 Hz.
The micro cable exhibited 15% to 30% higher dissipated energy (ΔED) and 20% to 47% higher equivalent damping factor (Δξ) compared to the monolithic wire due to inter-filament friction.

Structural fatigue life to first wire failure was shorter for the micro cable (~2000 cycles at frequencies ≥ 2 Hz) than for the monolithic wire (3000 to 6000 cycles) due to fretting friction and surface dimples.
The micro cable displayed progressive sequential failure across all 7 filaments, sustaining mechanical load and energy dissipation (up to ~1 MJ/m³) until the final wire broke.
modeling_methods: Calculation of dissipated energy per cycle (ED) via numerical integration of the stress-strain hysteresis loop (closed contour integral of σ dε).
Calculation of equivalent viscous damping factor (ξ) using the dissipated energy normalized by 4π times the equivalent linear stored elastic energy.
Identification of the critical self-heating frequency (fc) via interpolation of the zero-crossing of percentage peak stress difference (Δσ = 0) between the 1st and 128th cycles.
Linear Clausius-Clapeyron phase diagram regression to determine temperature stress coefficients CM (5.54 MPa/°C) and CA (6.28 MPa/°C).
Asymptotic non-linear regression modeling of cycle temperature amplitude (Tamp) as a function of loading frequency.
Linear regression modeling of 128th cycle mean temperature (Tmean) and cycles to failure (Nf) as functions of loading frequency.

possible_gap_implications: Understanding the self-heating threshold and dynamic thermomechanical stiffening in NiTi micro cables could inform frequency boundaries and thermal management strategies for SMA-based tendons or variable-stiffness components in dynamic structural and robotic applications, though robotic efficacy remains to be directly evaluated.
paper.research_objective: To investigate the effect of thermomechanical coupling and heat accumulation during dynamic tensile cycling (frequencies from 0.25 Hz to 10 Hz) on the mechanical behavior, functional damping properties, and fatigue life (both structural and functional) of NiTi SMA micro cables, determining the critical self-heating frequency and characterizing progressive individual filament failure relative to a solid reference wire.
paper.research_problem: The lack of understanding regarding the influence of high loading frequencies, strain rates, and cumulative self-heating on the functional energy dissipation properties, thermomechanical stiffening, and fatigue life of multi-strand NiTi shape memory alloy micro cables under dynamic cyclic loading.
stiffness_mechanism: thermomechanical coupling / temperature-induced stiffening governed by the Clausius-Clapeyron law
